title: 2: Stranded
text:
Introduction
Consider two seemingly unrelated scenarios:

You disagree vehemently with the market’s implied probabilities for the future. Assuming you’re right and the market’s wrong, do you have an edge? If so, how much?
A new asset is introduced to the market. Would trading it improve your long-run performance? If so, how much growth are you forgoing if you decline to trade it?

Knowing that this post will be about information theory, you may suspect that the answer to the first question is the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence \(D(p \| q)\) between your forecast \(p\) of the probabilities of future states and a risk-neutral probability measure, \(q\). This would imply that you have an edge whenever \(p \neq q\) since \(D\) is zero if and only if \(p = q\). You may also suspect that trading an additional asset would improve your long-run performance if and only if you could construct a portfolio with a higher Sharpe ratio. Neither claim is in general correct.
In spite of their apparent differences, these questions are closely related, as their answers fall out of the same information-theoretic framework, which I will derive in this post. The unifying thread is the idea of market incompleteness, which is the problem of not being able to bet on every possible future event. Because incompleteness implies the non-uniqueness of risk-neutral measures, this post can be thought of as an investigation into the implications of this non-uniqueness for the portfolio manager.
Both answers turn out to involve information projections. In particular, I’ll show that the rate at which you can beat cash in the long run is \(\min_{q \in \mathcal{Q}}D(p \| q)\), where \(\mathcal{Q}\) is the set of all risk-neutral measures. The naive answer \(D(p \| q)\) overestimates your edge by an amount I call the misfit, a phantom edge that can’t be captured by any portfolio. I derive these results and shed further light on them in What your disagreement with the market is worth. Then in What a missing asset is worth I show that the value of a new asset is precisely the misfit that adding it eliminates. I call this particular kind of misfit the stranded growth, which is evaluated at the optimal portfolio from the original market and the risk-neutral measure closest to \(p\) from the enlarged market. The stranded growth is positive if and only if the risk-neutral measure in the original market that is closest to \(p\) misprices the new asset. I also derive an approximation for the stranded growth in terms of the new asset’s appraisal ratio, and I demonstrate that while the stranded growth is related to the maximum Sharpe ratio, a new asset can increase the maximum Sharpe ratio while leaving the maximum growth rate unchanged, and vice versa.


Stranded at sea
Following the end of the Napoleonic Wars and the restoration of the Bourbon monarchy, on June 17, 1816, the French frigate La Méduse set sail for Saint-Louis to re-establish French colonial rule over Senegal. Captaining the ship was Hugues Duroy de Chaumareys, an aristocratic royalist émigré. By 1816 de Chaumareys had not captained a ship for two decades, and, eager to please the impatient colonial governor of Senegal, who was on board with him, he chose to ignore warnings from his officers and depart from the standard course, instead opting to take a more direct route that would bring the ship dangerously close to the shallow seas off the coast of present-day Mauritania.
On July 2, La Méduse ran aground roughly 30 miles off the coast. For three days her crew tried to dislodge the ship, but de Chaumareys refused to unburden her by jettisoning her cargo, which included 14 heavy cannons. To make matters worse, they had run aground during a spring high tide, so no later tide would rise high enough to float her off. It became clear that the ship could not be refloated, so on July 5 the captain called for her evacuation. There were not enough lifeboats for the over 400 people on board, however, so they salvaged timber from the ship to construct a makeshift raft for the 147 people who could not fit into a lifeboat. The 20-by-7-meter raft was thrown together haphazardly. It included a rudimentary sail but no rudder, and it was partially submerged under the weight of 147 people. The plan was for the lifeboats to tow the raft to shore.
For reasons that remain unclear, shortly after launch the towline connecting the raft with the lifeboats was severed. It was later alleged that this was a deliberate decision taken to ease the burden of those in the lifeboats. In any case, the 146 men and one woman on board the raft were suddenly adrift in open ocean on a partially submerged raft, with woefully inadequate provisions, no oars, no rudder, and a sail that hardly worked. Many of the horrors that ensued over the next 13 days were so lurid that I will not share them here. When the raft was finally rescued on July 17 by the Argus, another French ship accompanying La Méduse, only 15 of the original 147 people were still alive. Five of the 15 survivors would die from exhaustion shortly after reaching shore (Miles 2007).






Figure 1: Théodore Géricault, The Raft of the Medusa, 1819. Musée du Louvre. The painting depicts the raft’s survivors waving to the Argus on the distant horizon. Géricault’s assiduous preparation for this painting is the stuff of legend. He interviewed survivors, read published accounts, visited asylums and hospitals, studied the anatomy of corpses at a morgue – even bringing decaying body parts home with him for further inspection – and had a scale model of the raft constructed by one of the raft’s survivors, a carpenter. He made numerous preparatory studies, and when he was finally ready to put paint to canvas, he shaved his head and locked himself in his studio for eight months until he was done. When he emerged, the 27-year-old Géricault had created a 5-by-7-meter masterpiece that would shock the French establishment. What I find most interesting about this painting, however, isn’t Géricault’s talent or his obsessiveness (there are many talented eccentrics in the history of art); it is the scene Géricault chose to depict: he chose the precise moment when hope, uncertainty, tragedy, and death violently collide.





The setup

The basics
Let \(G \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times M}\) denote a matrix of gross returns for \(M\) assets over \(K\) possible future states of the world, where \(K > M\). I’ll refer to \(G\) as “the market.” By a gross return, I mean that if you invest one dollar in the \(j^{th}\) asset, then after one period that dollar has become \(G_{ij}\) dollars, assuming the \(i^{th}\) state is realized. I’ll let \(G_j\) denote the random gross return (payoff per dollar invested) of the \(j^{th}\) asset, which pays \(G_{ij}\) if the \(i^{th}\) state is realized. I’ll assume that the first asset, “cash,” is risk-free with gross return \(r\), i.e. the first column of \(G\) is \(r\mathbb{1}\), where \(\mathbb{1}\) is the vector of ones, of whatever length the context requires. I also assume that \(\operatorname{rank} G = M\), equivalently the linear map \(G: \mathbb{R}^M \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^K\) is injective.
I’ll let \(p = (p_1, \ldots, p_K)\) denote the probability vector that describes the likelihood of each of the states. Without loss of generality, I’ll assume \(p_i > 0\) for all \(1 \leq i \leq K\) (since otherwise we would just eliminate zero-probability states from consideration), so \(p\) resides within \(\Delta^{K-1}_{++} = \lbrace y \in \Delta^{K-1} : y_i > 0 \text{ for all } i \rbrace\), the set of strictly positive distributions, which is the relative interior of the probability simplex of \(K-1\) dimensions, \(\Delta^{K-1}\). We may think of \(p\) as known (given to us by, say, an oracle) or, more realistically, estimated based on research. In any case, it represents our belief as to the likelihood of future events. We will assume that \(p\) reflects reality, unless stated otherwise.
I’ll let \(\mathcal{A} = \lbrace w \in \mathbb{R}^M : \sum_{j=1}^M w_j = 1 \rbrace\) denote the set of all fully invested portfolios. The gross return of a portfolio \(w\) in the \(i^{th}\) state is \(Y_i(w) = \sum_{j=1}^M w_j G_{ij}\). I let \(Y(w)\) denote the random scalar equal to \(Y_i(w)\) in state \(i\).
We sample rows from \(G\) i.i.d. according to \(p\), and we fully reinvest our money after each period, rebalancing the portfolio weights so as to remain fixed at some \(w \in \mathcal{A}\). Note that if \(Y_i(w) \leq 0\) for any \(1 \leq i \leq K\), then we will eventually be ruined, as \(p_i > 0\) for all \(i\) by assumption, so it is useful to define \(\mathcal{A}_{++} = \lbrace w \in \mathcal{A} : Gw > 0 \rbrace\).
I will assume that \(G\) admits no arbitrage, meaning there is no position (unnormalized dollar holdings) \(x \in \mathbb{R}^M\) such that you can never lose money (\(Gx \geq 0\)), you have a chance at making money (\(Gx \neq 0\)), and you don’t need to invest anything (\(x^T \mathbb{1} \leq 0\)).
A market is said to be incomplete if \(G\) is not a surjective map: there exist payoffs (elements of the codomain \(\mathbb{R}^K\)) that can’t be reached by any position \(x \in \mathbb{R}^M\). It is precisely the fact that \(\operatorname{rank} G < K\) that causes market incompleteness.


Risk-neutral measures
The first part of the Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing (FTAP) says that a market admits no arbitrage if and only if there exists a strictly positive pricing vector \(\psi \in \mathbb{R}^K\) such that \(G^T \psi = \mathbb{1}\), where \(\psi_i\) is the price today of a claim that pays \(\$1\) tomorrow if the \(i^{th}\) state is realized and pays nothing otherwise (Harrison and Pliska 1981). This means that the price of the \(j^{th}\) asset is \(\$1\) for all \(1 \leq j \leq M\). The prices are all exactly \(\$1\) because \(G\) contains gross returns rather than absolute payoffs. Therefore, the first part of the FTAP says that no arbitrage is equivalent to the existence of some strictly positive probability measure \(q\) such that \(G^T q = \frac{1}{c}\mathbb{1}\), where \(c = \sum_{i=1}^K \psi_i\). Whenever there is a risk-free rate (as is our case), we have \(c = 1/r\); hence, no arbitrage is equivalent to the existence of some strictly positive probability measure \(q\) such that \(G^T q = r\mathbb{1}\). Now, define \(\mathcal{Q} = \mathcal{Q}(G)\) to be the set of all probability measures \(q\) that exist within the affine space given by \[
G^T q = r\mathbb{1}.
\tag{1}\] By the rank–nullity theorem, this affine space has dimension \(K - M\). Elements of \(\mathcal{Q}\) are called risk-neutral probability measures and are said to be consistent with market prices. They are said to be risk-neutral because every asset has the same expected gross return, namely \(r\), the same as cash, so an investor who is indifferent to risk and who believes \(q\) to be the true distribution would be indifferent to the \(M\) assets. In addition, let \(\mathcal{Q}_{++} = \lbrace q \in \mathcal{Q} : q > 0 \rbrace\), the elements of which are called equivalent martingale measures (EMMs). Relative to cash, assets are priced correctly under all \(q \in \mathcal{Q}\), meaning \(\mathbb{E}_q \left[ \frac{G_j}{r} \right] = 1\) for all \(j\), which follows from Equation 1. The unit of account, in this case cash, is called a numeraire.
It follows from the injectivity of \(G\) and Jensen’s inequality that for every \(q \in \mathcal{Q}_{++}\), there exists some \(j\) such that \(\mathbb{E}_q \left[\frac{G_j}{Y(w)} \right] \neq 1\) when \(w \in \mathcal{A}_{++}\) isn’t cash. There is, however, a different measure that prices assets correctly using \(w \in \mathcal{A}_{++}\) as the numeraire, which I define in The tilted measure.
A stochastic discount factor (SDF) is defined as a random scalar \(\xi\) satisfying \(\mathbb{E}_p [\xi G_j] = 1\) for all \(j\). It is straightforward to show that there exists a strictly positive SDF \(\xi\) if and only if there exists some \(q \in \mathcal{Q}_{++}\); their relationship is simple: \(\xi_i = \frac{q_i}{r p_i}\). This implies that if \(p \in \mathcal{Q}\), then \(\frac{1}{r}\) is a (strictly positive) SDF for \(p\).
Using this terminology, the first part of the FTAP says that the condition of no arbitrage is equivalent to the existence of at least one EMM. Given no arbitrage, the second part of the FTAP says that an EMM is unique if and only if the market is complete. We could replace “EMM” in each of these statements with “strictly positive SDF.” Our market is incomplete, so there are infinitely many EMMs. This post is about the consequences of this non-uniqueness.


Our goal
The expected log return, i.e. the growth rate, is defined for all \(w \in \mathcal{A}_{++}\) as
\[\begin{aligned}
W(w) = \sum_{i=1}^K p_i \ln Y_i(w),
\end{aligned} \tag{2}\]
in nats (1 nat = \(1 / \ln 2\) bits). For all \(w \not \in \mathcal{A}_{++}\), we take \(W(w) = -\infty\) since \(p_i > 0\) for all \(i\). Our goal is to maximize \(W\) over \(\mathcal{A}\) because the growth rate determines the long-run, almost-sure performance of a portfolio, as I showed in my first post. This is called log-optimal investing, which is also known as growth-optimal investing and Kelly investing (Kelly 1956). In order to emphasize the dependence on the distribution \(p\), I will sometimes write \(W_p(w)\) for the growth rate. We can achieve at least \(W_p = \ln r\) by using the risk-free asset; thus our goal is to improve upon this minimum level of performance. I let \(w_p^*\) denote the optimizer (or just \(w^*\) when \(p\) is understood), which is called the log-optimal portfolio. In a future post, I will prove that such an optimum exists if and only if there is no arbitrage. Since we are assuming no arbitrage, an optimum exists (see also Vecer 2026, Lemma 9 and Theorem 10). In addition, the optimum is unique, as shown below.






Figure 2: Albrecht Dürer, Salvator Mundi, ca. 1505. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Writing in his Naturalis Historia (Section 35.145) over fourteen centuries before Dürer, the Roman author Pliny the Elder observed that incomplete works of art are often more admired than completed ones because the viewer can see the preliminary outlines used to scaffold the painting and perceive the thoughts of a master at work (“in maiore admiratione esse quam perfecta; quippe in iis liniamenta reliqua ipsaeque cogitationes artificum spectantur”). In this work, Dürer’s “liniamenta” – the underlying drawing beneath the paint’s surface – are clearly visible in Christ’s face and also his right hand.






What your disagreement with the market is worth
This section answers the first question: if your forecasted probability measure is \(p\), how much is your edge? It turns out that although \(D(p \| q)\) plays an important role, it is not the edge, only an upper bound on it.

The first-order condition
Now we’re ready to get down to work. Recall that our goal is to maximize \(W(w)\) subject to the budget constraint \(\sum_{j=1}^M w_j = 1\). To solve this problem, we introduce the Lagrangian with multiplier \(\lambda\) given by \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}(w, \lambda) = -\sum_{i=1}^K p_i \ln Y_i(w) + \lambda \left(\sum_{j=1}^M w_j - 1 \right).
\end{aligned}
\] Setting the gradient with respect to \(w\) equal to zero yields a condition for the multiplier: \(\sum_{i=1}^K p_i \frac{G_{ij}}{Y_i(w^*)} = \lambda\). Upon multiplying both sides by the portfolio weights and summing over all \(M\) assets, we find that \(\lambda = 1\); hence, we obtain a necessary first-order condition (FOC) for a portfolio to be optimal: \[
\sum_{i=1}^K p_i \frac{G_{ij}}{Y_i(w^*)} = 1,
\tag{3}\] which is to hold for every \(1 \leq j \leq M\). From the FOC we see that for all \(w \in \mathcal{A}\) \[
\mathbb{E}_p \left[ \frac{Y(w)}{Y(w^*)}\right] = 1.
\tag{4}\] Conversely, suppose some portfolio \(w' \in \mathcal{A}_{++}\) satisfies the FOC so that \(\mathbb{E}_p \left[ \frac{Y(w)}{Y(w')} \right] = 1\) for all \(w \in \mathcal{A}\). It then follows from Jensen’s inequality that \(W(w') \geq W(w)\) for all \(w\); hence \(w'\) optimizes the growth rate: the FOC is also sufficient for optimality. Thus, a portfolio optimizes the growth rate if and only if it satisfies the FOC. Moreover, since the growth rate is a strictly concave function of \(w\) whenever \(G\) is injective, we see that the optimizer is unique. The optimality of \(w^*\) together with Jensen’s inequality reveals that for any \(w \in \mathcal{A}_{++}\) \[
\mathbb{E}_p \left[ \frac{Y(w^*)}{Y(w)} \right] \geq 1,
\] which is another sense in which \(w^*\) is an optimal portfolio.
The positivity of \(Y(w^*)\) together with Equation 4 implies that \(\xi^* = \frac{1}{Y(w^*)}\) is an SDF under the law of \(p\). In other words, measured in units of the log-optimal portfolio (i.e. \(w^*\) is the numeraire), every portfolio is correctly priced under the belief \(p\), where the reader will recall that the price of every asset (and therefore portfolio) is \(1\) (Long 1990). In addition, because \(w^*\) is unique, it follows from Jensen’s inequality that \(\xi^*\) is the only positive SDF that can be expressed as the inverse of a portfolio’s gross return.


A special risk-neutral probability measure
Upon multiplying both sides of Equation 3 by \(r\), we find:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^K \left(p_i \frac{r}{Y_i(w^*)}\right) G_{ij} = r,
\end{aligned}
\] which also holds for every \(j\). Moreover, since the first column of \(G\) is \(r\mathbb{1}\), we have by Equation 3, \(\sum_{i=1}^K p_i \frac{r}{Y_i(w^*)} = 1\). This leads us to define the function \(q^*: \Delta^{K-1}_{++} \rightarrow \mathcal{Q}_{++}\) whose \(i^{th}\) component is given by \[
\begin{aligned}
q_i^* = p_i \frac{r}{Y_i(w_p^*)}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}\] We see that \(q^*\) is the measure induced by \(p\) when we switch the numeraire from the optimal portfolio to the risk-free asset: \(\mathbb{E}_{q^*}[Y(w) / r] = 1\) holds for every \(w\), where \(1\) is the price of every asset (and therefore every portfolio).


The edge
Solving Equation 5 for \(Y_i(w^*)\) and substituting into Equation 2 we see that the optimum growth rate is, up to the constant \(\ln r\), given by the information divergence from the model distribution \(q^*\) to the true (well, believed) distribution \(p\):
\[\begin{aligned}
\boxed{\rule[-1ex]{0pt}{4ex} W(w^*) = \ln r + D(p\| q^*)}
\end{aligned} \tag{6}\] where the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence is defined, for any two distributions \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) on the \(K\) states, by \(D(\mu \| \nu) = \sum_i \mu_i \ln \frac{\mu_i}{\nu_i}\) in nats, where \(0 \ln \frac{0}{\nu_i} = 0\) and where \(D(\mu \| \nu) = \infty\) if \(\mu\) is not absolutely continuous with respect to \(\nu\), i.e. if there exists some \(i\) such that both \(\mu_i > 0\) and \(\nu_i = 0\). KL divergence measures how well \(\nu\) models \(\mu\) (lower KL is better; 0 is perfect), and in base 2 represents the expected excess number of bits needed to code/represent the output of a random source \(\mu\) using a code optimized for \(\nu\). It is therefore a measure of the inefficiency of using \(\nu\) as your model when \(\mu\) is the true measure.
If \(W(w^*) - \ln r > 0\), then we have an edge, which measured in nats per period is given by \(D(p \| q^*)\).
Of course, our belief \(p\) is only a best guess for some true distribution \(\tau\), so our true growth rate will not be \(W_p(w_p^*)\); instead it will be \(W_{\tau}(w_p^*)\). To find an expression for \(W_{\tau}(w_p^*)\), we can use our definition of \(q^*\) to solve for \(Y_i(w_p^*)\), which when plugged into the growth rate formula (Equation 2) yields \[
\begin{aligned}
W_{\tau}(w_p^*) &= \ln r + D(\tau \| q_p^*) - D(\tau \| p), \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}\] where I write \(q_p^*\) to emphasize that \(q^*\) is a function of \(p\). Equation 7 implies that you can beat cash if and only if your belief \(p\) is closer to reality than your pricing measure \(q_p^*\). This generalizes a similar formula in Section 6.1 of Cover and Thomas (2006) to the case where markets are incomplete.


An alternative characterization of \(q^*\)
We started off this section asking whether the edge was \(D(p \| q)\) and we discovered that it is in fact \(D(p \| q^*)\). We can now use our formula for the edge to shed light on the nature of \(D(p \| q)\) for \(q \in \mathcal{Q}_{++}\) (see also Vecer 2026, Remark 11): \[
\begin{aligned}
D(p \| q^*) &= \sum_i p_i \ln \left( \frac{p_i q_i}{q_i^* q_i} \right) \\
&= D(p \| q) - \sum_i p_i \ln \left( \frac{q_i^*}{q_i} \right) \\
&= D(p \| q) - \sum_i p_i \ln \left( \frac{p_i}{q_i Y_i(w^*) / r} \right) \\
& \leq D(p \| q),
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}\] where the inequality follows from the fact that \(\sum_i q_i Y_i(w^*) / r = 1\) (since \(\mathbb{E}_q[Y(w)] = r\) holds for any risk-neutral measure \(q \in \mathcal{Q}\) and \(w \in \mathcal{A}\)), which implies that the sum is a KL divergence, and thus is never negative. The above inequality continues to hold when \(q_i = 0\) for some \(i\); thus, we have deduced that for every \(q \in \mathcal{Q}\), \(D(p \| q)\) is an upper bound on the edge, implying \[
\begin{aligned}
W(w^*) \leq \ln r + D(p \| q),
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}\] which is a specific instance of a more general inequality involving stochastic discount factors (Bansal and Lehmann 1997). Now, from Equation 9 and recalling Equation 6, we see that (Vecer 2026, Lemma 9 and Theorem 10) \[
\max_{w \in \mathcal{A}} W(w) = \ln r + \min_{q \in \mathcal{Q}} D(p \| q),
\tag{10}\] hence, since \(D(p \|q)\) is strictly convex in its second argument, our special risk-neutral measure is the reverse information projection of our belief onto \(\mathcal{Q}\): \[
q^* = \arg \min_{q \in \mathcal{Q}} D(p \| q),
\tag{11}\] where “reverse” refers to the fact that the optimization occurs over the second argument (Csiszár and Matúš 2003).
In Equation 5 we defined \(q^*\) as the measure induced from \(p\) by changing numeraire from the log-optimal portfolio to the risk-free asset, and then we derived Equation 11. We could have gone the other way, however, and defined \(q^*\) in terms of Equation 11 and then deduced that \(q^*\) is given by Equation 5. We are therefore entitled to think about \(q^*\) in terms of numeraires or in terms of information theory; they are equivalent: \[
q_i^* = p_i \frac{r}{Y_i(w_p^*)} \iff q^* = \arg \min_{q \in \mathcal{Q}} D(p \| q).
\]


You have to be able to trade your disagreement
We are now in a position to offer more insight into when there is or is not an edge. Because we have an edge if and only if \(D(p \| q^*) > 0 \iff p \neq q^* \iff p \not \in \mathcal{Q}\), to see if we have an edge, we can simply check if \(\mathbb{E}_p[G_j] \neq r\) for some \(j\): check if, under your beliefs, any asset has a nonzero expected excess return. This is equivalent to asking whether \(p\) is not in the affine space defined by Equation 1, i.e. \(p \not \in q + \operatorname{null} G^T\) for any \(q \in \mathcal{Q}\). Think of \(p - q\) as the “disagreement” between \(p\) and \(q\). Because \((\operatorname{col} G)^{\perp} = \operatorname{null} G^T\), the decomposition of this disagreement given by \[\begin{aligned}
p - q = u + v,
\end{aligned}\] where \(u \in \operatorname{col} G\) and \(v \in \operatorname{null} G^T\), is unique, and therefore \(u\) is independent of our choice for \(q\), since for any \(q, q' \in \mathcal{Q}\), \(q - q' \in \operatorname{null} G^T\). We therefore have a positive edge if and only if \(u \neq 0\); thus, disagreeing with any particular risk-neutral measure is not enough: there’s an edge if and only if there is a component of the disagreement contained within \(\operatorname{col} G\). Put differently, it is not enough to simply disagree with the market: you have an edge if and only if your disagreement is tradable.






Figure 3: Leonardo da Vinci, Adoration of the Magi, 1481–1482. Uffizi Gallery. Leonardo left most of his works unfinished. This is often put down to perfectionism, but it likely owed as much to his insatiable curiosity, which led him to ask questions and begin new projects at an incalculable pace. This leads us to ask whether art is better thought of as a process than as a finished state. A news article on the Uffizi Gallery website goes even further, arguing, “A singular fate has marked the destiny of almost all of Leonardo da Vinci’s works. None of them, it would seem, according to the current state of scholarship, was ever brought to completion by the artist; all remained unfinished to varying degrees” (my translation).





The tilted measure (change of numeraire)
Recall that in An alternative characterization of \(q^*\) I mentioned \(\sum_i q_i Y_i(w^*) / r = 1\). This motivates us to define a new probability measure: \(m: \mathcal{Q}_{++} \times \mathcal{A}_{++} \rightarrow \Delta^{K-1}_{++},\) where \[
\begin{aligned}
m_i(q, w) = q_i \frac{Y_i(w)}{r},
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}\] from which we see that \(m\) is \(q\) after reweighting state by state and then renormalizing: it is as if \(q\) has been “tilted.”
Notice that \(q\) and \(m\) are equivalent as probability measures (i.e. \(m_i = 0 \iff q_i = 0\)). Whereas \(q\) has the risk-free asset (with gross return \(r\)) as its associated numeraire, \(m\) has the portfolio \(w\) (with gross return \(Y(w)\)) as its associated numeraire. This implies \[
\mathbb{E}_m \left[ \frac{G_j}{Y(w)} \right] = 1,
\tag{13}\] for all \(j\), meaning that \(m\) prices every asset correctly using \(w\) as the numeraire. Because we established earlier that a portfolio \(w\) satisfies the FOC (Equation 3) if and only if it is optimal, Equation 13 implies \(w\) is the optimal portfolio for \(m\). We also see that \(q = \arg \min_{q' \in \mathcal{Q}}D(m(q,w) \| q')\) since \(q\) is a change of numeraire from the optimal \(w\) (under the law \(m\)) to cash, analogous to our definition of \(q^*\). The measure \(m(q,w)\) is the unique belief under which \(w\) is the optimal portfolio and whose projection onto \(\mathcal{Q}\) is \(q\).
Finally, notice that by setting \(q = q^*\), we can chain our two change-of-numeraire formulas, \(q^*\) followed by \(m\), in which case \(m(q^*, w)\) can be understood as the measure induced by \(p\) when we switch numeraire from \(w^*\) to some arbitrary \(w\). It follows that \(m(q^*, w^*) = p\).


The decomposition formula for naive edge
We can now express the equality embedded within Equation 8 as \[
\begin{aligned}
\boxed{\rule[-1ex]{0pt}{4ex} D(p \| q) = D(p \| q^*) + D(p \| m(q, w^*))}
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}\] which can be thought of as \[
\text{naive edge} = \text{edge} + \text{misfit},
\] where I’m defining misfit as \(D(p \| m(q, w^*))\), i.e. how poorly \(m(q, w^*)\) models your actual belief \(p\). We can also think of it as a phantom edge, as it bridges the gap between the growth we might intuitively think we can achieve and what we can actually achieve. The misfit arises from using a belief which differs from \(p\) only because it uses a different risk-neutral measure, as both \(m(q, w^*)\) and \(p = m(q^*, w^*)\) agree on the optimum portfolio. Finally, I note that another way to view the misfit is as an expected log likelihood ratio: \(D(p \| m(q, w^*)) = \mathbb{E}_p \left[ \ln \frac{q^*}{q} \right]\).


The growth-rate formula
By now we have seen that \(m(q^*, w^*) = p\) and that \(m(q, w^*)\) is the tilted measure used to define the misfit. In addition, I remarked that \(m(q^*, w)\) is the measure resulting from \(p\) due to changing numeraire from \(w^*\) to some arbitrary \(w\). There is a deeper significance though: \[
W(w^*) - W(w) = \mathbb{E}_p \left[ \ln \frac{Y(w^*)}{Y(w)} \right] = D(p \| m(q^*, w)).
\tag{15}\] In other words, \(D(p \| m(q^*, w))\) is the growth shortfall. This implies that the edge is the growth shortfall of the all-cash portfolio: \(D(p \| m(q^*, \text{cash})) = D(p \| q^*)\).
To see the broader, information-theoretic meaning of \(m(q,w)\) for arbitrary \(q\) and \(w\), we can solve Equation 12 for \(Y_i(w)\) and substitute it into Equation 2 to yield a formula for the growth rate \(W_p(w)\), which holds for every \(q \in \mathcal{Q}_{++}\) and \(w \in \mathcal{A}_{++}\): \[\begin{aligned}
\boxed{\rule[-1ex]{0pt}{4ex} W_p(w) = \ln r + D(p \| q) - D(p \| m(q,w))}
\end{aligned}
\tag{16}\] which is independent of the choice of \(q\) (see also Vecer 2026, eq. 11, where \(r=1\)). This generalizes the final boxed equation in my first post to account for market incompleteness.


Naive growth
Combining these results we see that if we think of \(\ln r + D(p \| q)\) as naive growth, then we really have three tiers of growth given by \(W(w) \leq W(w^*) \leq \ln r + D(p \| q)\): \[
W(w) \xrightarrow{D(p \| m(q^*, w))} W(w^*) \xrightarrow{D(p \| m(q, w^*))} \ln r + D(p \| q),
\tag{17}\] where \[
D(p \| m(q^*, w)) + D(p \| m(q, w^*)) = D(p \| m(q, w)).
\tag{18}\] The growth shortfall in Equation 17 is under the control of the investor, as you simply need to improve the portfolio; however, for a given \(q \neq q^*\), no amount of portfolio optimization can eliminate the misfit, which is a product of the market itself, since \(\mathcal{Q}\) is a function of \(G\). From Equation 16 and Equation 18 we therefore see that the misfit acts as a floor on the gap between our hoped-for growth rate, \(\ln r + D(p \| q)\), and our actual growth rate, and that the floor is achieved by taking \(w = w^*\).
I’ve just shown that \(D(p \| m(q, w^*)) = \min_{w \in \mathcal{A}_{++}} D(p \| m(q, w))\). More can be said about \(m(q, w^*)\) though. Let \(\mathcal{M}_{q,\,\cdot}\) denote the image of the function \(w \mapsto m(q, w)\). As the image of a linear function over a convex set, \(\mathcal{M}_{q,\,\cdot}\) is itself a convex set. This, together with the strict convexity of KL divergence in its second argument, implies that \(m(q, w^*)\) is unique as an optimizing tilted measure; thus, \(m(q, w^*)\) is the reverse information projection of \(p\) onto \(\mathcal{M}_{q,\,\cdot}\), \[
m(q, w^*) = \arg \min_{m' \in \mathcal{M}_{q,\,\cdot}} D(p \| m').
\tag{19}\] Moreover, because \(G\) is injective, so is \(w \mapsto m(q, w)\), and therefore \(w^*\) is the only portfolio that achieves the minimum: \(w^* = \arg \min_{w \in \mathcal{A}_{++}} D(p \| m(q, w))\).

What a missing asset is worth
I’ll now answer the second question by measuring the extra growth rate achieved by trading an additional asset. I’ll also contrast the results I derive with a more familiar approach involving Sharpe ratios. In general, trading an additional asset shrinks \(\mathcal{Q}\), so the machinery we developed in the previous section turns out to be very pertinent for figuring out how much growth we forgo by not trading it.

The seesaw
Both sides of the duality expressed by Equation 10 implicitly depend on \(G\), the left side via the definition of the growth rate, and the right side via the definition of \(\mathcal{Q}\). In particular, the minimum achieved on the right-hand side of Equation 10 never decreases as the set \(\mathcal{Q}\) contracts.
Let \(G' \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times (M+1)}\) be \(G\) with one added column, \(\gamma\), which is linearly independent of the columns of \(G\). As with \(G\), we assume the market defined by \(G'\) admits no arbitrage. Observe that \(\mathcal{Q}(G') = \lbrace q \in \mathcal{Q}(G): \mathbb{E}_q[\gamma] = r \rbrace\), and since we are assuming \(\gamma\) is linearly independent of all the columns in \(G\) (and since \(\mathcal{Q}_{++}(G) \neq \emptyset\)), we have \(\mathcal{Q}(G') \subsetneq \mathcal{Q}(G)\). We have, in effect, a seesaw: expand the number of tradable assets (columns in \(G\)), contract the set \(\mathcal{Q}\) – and vice versa.


Stranded growth
I’ll let \(q^*_G = \arg \min_{q \in \mathcal{Q}(G)} D(p \| q)\) and analogously for \(q^*_{G'}.\) If \(\mathbb{E}_{q^*_G}[\gamma] = r\) happens to hold, i.e. if \(\gamma\) is correctly priced under \(q_G^*\), then \(q_G^*\) is a member of \(\mathcal{Q}(G')\); therefore, since \(q_{G}^*\) is the minimizer over the superset \(\mathcal{Q}(G)\), we have \(q_{G'}^* = q_{G}^*\) and our edge remains at \(D(p \| q_{G'}^*) = D(p \| q_G^*)\): \(\gamma\) is not a binding constraint for the minimization over \(\mathcal{Q}\). On the other hand, if \(\mathbb{E}_{q^*_G}[\gamma] \neq r\), then \(q_G^* \not \in \mathcal{Q}(G')\) – \(\gamma\) acts as a further constraint for the minimization over \(\mathcal{Q}\) – and therefore \(q^*_{G'} \neq q^*_G\). By the uniqueness of the reverse information projection, we see that our edge increases to \(D(p \| q_{G'}^*) > D(p \| q_{G}^*)\). Succinctly, \(D(p \| q^*_{G'}) \geq D(p \| q^*_G)\), which is strict – trading the new asset is beneficial – if and only if \[
\mathbb{E}_{q^*_G}[\gamma] \neq r,
\tag{20}\] which constitutes a simple criterion for whether or not to trade a new asset. This is equivalent to asking whether \(\mathbb{E}_{p}[\xi^* \gamma] \neq 1\), where you will recall \(\xi^*_i = 1 / Y_i(w_G^*)\) is the SDF arising from the FOC (Equation 3).
By contrast, it has traditionally been considered beneficial to trade a new asset if doing so would expand the mean-variance frontier of the available assets. When there exists a risk-free asset, this reduces to the criterion \(\alpha \neq 0\), where \(\alpha\) is the intercept that arises from regressing the new asset’s excess return on those of the risky assets of \(G\) (Huberman and Kandel 1987). These criteria are not equivalent, as seen in Table 1.

Suppose now that we start with \(G'\) and remove \(\gamma\) from it, leaving us with \(G\), and let \(w^*_G\) denote the log-optimal portfolio for the market \(G\) and analogously for \(G'\). From Equation 10 we see that we can express the decline in the maximum growth rate – which can be thought of as growth that is inaccessible, forgone, or stranded – as \[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma &= W(w_{G'}^*) - W(w_{G}^*) \\
&= D(p \| q^*_{G'}) - D(p \| q^*_G).
\end{aligned}
\tag{21}\]
Let’s focus now on the market \(G\). Recall that \(q_{G'}^* \in \mathcal{Q}_{++}(G)\) since \(\mathcal{Q}(G') \subset \mathcal{Q}(G)\) and \(q^*\) is always positive by construction (Equation 5). Applying the decomposition formula (Equation 14), we find \[
\begin{aligned}
D(p \| q^*_{G'}) = D(p \| q^*_G) + D(p \| m(q^*_{G'}, w^*_{G})),
\end{aligned}
\] hence, \[
\boxed{\rule[-1ex]{0pt}{4ex} \sigma = D \left( p \| m(q^*_{G'}, w^*_{G}) \right)}
\tag{22}\] In words, the decomposition reads \[
\text{expanded market edge} = \text{edge} + \text{stranded growth}.
\] The stranded term is just the misfit from the decomposition formula that occurs when the market’s risk-neutral measure comes from the expanded market \(G'\) rather than \(G\). We also see that, as a misfit, \[
\sigma = \mathbb{E}_p \left[ \ln \frac{q^*_G}{q^*_{G'}} \right],
\tag{23}\] which makes clear that \(\sigma\) is a reflection of how dissimilar \(q^*_{G'}\) and \(q^*_{G}\) are, as seen from \(p\).
In our running example, which is illustrated in Figure 4, adding the asset \(\gamma = (0.5, 0.7, 1.7)\) to the base market completes the market, causing \(\mathcal{Q}(G)\) to collapse to the singleton \(\mathcal{Q}(G') = \lbrace \tilde{q} \rbrace\). In that case, \(q^*_{G'}\) is trivially equal to \(\tilde{q}\), so \(\sigma = D(p \| \tilde{m}) \approx 0.276\) nats, where \(\tilde{m} = m(q^*_{G'}, w^*_{G})\).
If we swap our perspective from that of \(G\) to that of \(G'\), then we interpret \(\sigma\) not as a misfit but as the growth shortfall that occurs when we use a portfolio optimized for \(G\). To see this, note that \(w_G^*\) can be embedded within \(\mathbb{R}^{M+1}\) by simply appending a zero. If \(\sigma > 0\), then, in this expanded market, \(w_{G'}^*\) is optimal, not \(w_G^*\), so by recalling the definition of growth shortfall (Equation 15) we arrive once again at Equation 22.
We now have two ways of understanding the stranded growth: from the perspective of \(G\) it is a misfit; from that of \(G'\) it is a growth shortfall. In either case, we can think of \(\sigma\) as the cost of incompleteness attributable to the removal of \(\gamma\). Viewed from the opposite perspective, \(\sigma\) is the increase in the growth rate that comes from trading the extra asset: \(\sigma\) answers the second of the two questions from the Introduction.


Comparison with Sharpe
For any non-cash portfolio \(w\), we can define the Sharpe ratio, \(SR(w) = \frac{\mathbb{E}[R(w)]}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[R(w)]}}\), where \(R(w) = Y(w) - r\) denotes the excess return over cash and where the expectations are under \(p\). Portfolio managers around the world aim to increase their portfolio’s Sharpe ratio, as higher values are associated with greater returns per unit of risk – at least if risk is defined as the standard deviation of excess returns.
I define \(S(G) = \max_{w \in \mathcal{A}, \, w \neq \text{cash}} SR(w)\) to be the maximum achievable Sharpe ratio by trading the assets from \(G\). Let \(R_{\gamma}\) denote the new risky asset’s excess return above cash, and let \(e \in \mathbb{R}^{M-1}\) denote the excess return vector for the risky assets in \(G\). Now, regress \(R_{\gamma}\) on \(e\): \[
R_{\gamma} = \alpha + \beta^T e + \epsilon,
\] where \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are chosen so that both \(\mathbb{E}_p[\epsilon] = 0\) and \(\epsilon\) is uncorrelated with \(e\). We can create a hedged asset that is long the new asset and short \(\beta\) units of the risky assets such that \(R_{\gamma} - \beta^T e = \alpha + \epsilon\) is the excess return of the hedged asset, which is then uncorrelated with the \(M-1\) other risky assets. Treynor and Black (1973) showed that \[
S(G')^2 = S(G)^2 + A^2,
\] where \(A = \frac{\alpha}{\text{std}(\epsilon)}\) is the appraisal ratio for the new asset. From this equation we see that an investor whose goal is to maximize his Sharpe ratio will trade the additional asset if and only if \(\alpha \neq 0\).
Under conditions where \(S(G), \, S(G') \ll 1\) and the excess returns are approximately Gaussian, a second-order Taylor approximation reveals \(W(w_G^*) \approx \ln r + \frac{1}{2}S(G)^2\). We can approximate \(W(w_{G'}^*)\) similarly. By definition \(\sigma = W(w_{G'}^*) - W(w_{G}^*)\), so, with the Treynor-Black identity, it follows that, under these conditions, \[
\boxed{\rule[-1ex]{0pt}{4ex} \sigma \approx \frac{1}{2}A^2}
\tag{24}\]
The approximation of Equation 24 can break down when these conditions no longer hold. For example, in Table 1 I consider a base market, \(G\), consisting of cash and one risky asset, \(a\), and I analyze what happens by adding one of two new assets in order to complete the market, either \(\gamma^{(1)}\) or \(\gamma^{(2)}\). The expanded – indeed, completed – market, \(G'\), is either \([G \;\, \gamma^{(1)}]\) or \([G \;\, \gamma^{(2)}]\). In this example, \(S(G)^2 \approx 0.24\), and \(S(G')^2 \approx 0.24\) or \(0.26\) for \(\gamma^{(1)}\) and \(\gamma^{(2)}\) respectively, neither of which is small. In addition, the distribution of excess returns in this three-state market is not well approximated by a Gaussian distribution; thus, skew and higher moments matter. It is no surprise, therefore, that \(\sigma - \frac{1}{2}A^2\) is not approximately zero, equaling \(0.00694\) and \(-0.00780\) for \([G \;\, \gamma^{(1)}]\) and \([G \;\, \gamma^{(2)}]\) respectively.
Both \(\gamma^{(1)}\) and \(\gamma^{(2)}\) have an expected excess return of zero under \(p\). I also consider two portfolio managers (PMs), the first of whom is a log-optimal investor. The second seeks to maximize his Sharpe ratio, but this does not identify a unique portfolio as Sharpe ratios are independent of leverage. To pin down a portfolio, our Sharpe-optimal PM chooses his leverage so as to maximize his growth rate – the most charitable choice for comparison. The log-optimal PM asks whether the new asset is correctly priced under \(q_G^*\) (Equation 20), the Sharpe-optimal PM whether \(\alpha = 0\) (Huberman and Kandel 1987).
Both PMs agree that the optimal portfolio for the base market is \((0.277, 0.723)\) for cash and the risky asset respectively. They agree because every portfolio that is long in \(a\) will have the same Sharpe ratio, so the secondary optimization over leverage lands the Sharpe-optimal portfolio on the log-optimal one. Once a second risky asset becomes available to trade, however, their assessments diverge, as the log-optimal PM prefers to have \(\gamma^{(1)}\) added to \(G\), the Sharpe-optimal PM \(\gamma^{(2)}\). The log-optimal PM trades \(\gamma^{(1)}\), increasing his growth rate by \(0.00694\) nats per period compared to \(G\), but sees no use for \(\gamma^{(2)}\) as trading it cannot increase his growth rate. Conversely, the Sharpe-optimal PM increases his Sharpe ratio by \(0.0156\) by trading \(\gamma^{(2)}\) compared to \(G\), but he doesn’t touch \(\gamma^{(1)}\) as it can’t be used to increase his Sharpe ratio.
Judged by his own criterion, each PM is satisfied – the log-optimal PM increases his growth rate, Sharpe-optimal his Sharpe ratio – but judged by the other’s criterion, they fare worse. In particular, when the log-optimal PM trades \(\gamma^{(1)}\) he ends up decreasing his Sharpe ratio by 0.00767 (from 0.492 for \(G\) to 0.485 for \([G \;\, \gamma^{(1)}]\)), and when the Sharpe-optimal PM trades \(\gamma^{(2)}\) he decreases his growth rate by 0.00616 nats per period (from 0.0929 for \(G\) to 0.0867 for \([G \;\, \gamma^{(2)}]\)). Whether their clients care will depend on which number they read.

def log_optimal(G, p, tol=1e-12, max_iter=100):
    """Log-optimal weights w (sum w = 1) for a K x M gross-return matrix G whose
    column 0 is cash. Damped Newton on the risky weights x, w = (1 - sum x, x),
    so Y = G w = r + (G[:, 1:] - r) x; backtracking keeps Y > 0. Returns w, Y and
    the largest first-order-condition residual max_j |sum_i p_i G_ij / Y_i - 1|
    (@eq-foc) over every asset, cash included."""
    X = G[:, 1:] - G[:, [0]]
    x = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for _ in range(max_iter):
        Y = G[:, 0] + X @ x
        grad = X.T @ (p / Y)
        if np.max(np.abs(grad)) < tol:
            break
        H = -(X * (p / Y**2)[:, None]).T @ X
        step = np.linalg.solve(H, -grad)
        t = 1.0
        while np.any(G[:, 0] + X @ (x + t * step) <= 0):
            t *= 0.5
        x = x + t * step
    w = np.concatenate([[1.0 - x.sum()], x])
    Y = G @ w
    return w, Y, float(np.max(np.abs(G.T @ (p / Y) - 1.0)))

def mean_cov(R, p):
    """Mean vector and covariance matrix under p of the columns of R (K x n)."""
    mu = p @ R
    D = R - mu
    return mu, (D * p[:, None]).T @ D


def max_sharpe(R, p, r):

    Sigma^-1 mu (mu = excess means over r), every positive multiple of which attains it."""
    mu, S = mean_cov(R, p)
    z = np.linalg.solve(S, mu - r)
    return float(np.sqrt((mu - r) @ z)), z


def sharpe(Y, p, r):
    """Sharpe ratio E_p[Y - r] / std_p(Y - r) of payoff Y, all moments under p."""
    ex = Y - r
    return float((p @ ex) / np.sqrt(p @ (ex - p @ ex)**2))

    """Sharpe-optimal weights: the tangency direction z (risky weights; every positive
    multiple has the maximum Sharpe ratio) levered by the lam > 0 that maximizes the growth
    rate E_p[ln(r + lam d)], d = (G[:, 1:] - r) z. Its derivative E_p[d / (r + lam d)]

    every payoff positive, so bisection pins down its unique root to machine precision.

    d = (G[:, 1:] - r) @ z                              # excess payoff per unit of lam

    x = lo * z
    w = np.concatenate([[1.0 - x.sum()], x])
    return w, G @ w, deriv(lo)

Conclusion

There are no rules any more. I’m just numb to what would have been jaw-dropping events for me a year ago. At some point, maybe I’ll get hit by a whole wave of PTSD.
— Terence Tao, quoted in Bumiller (2026)

The Fields Medal-winning mathematician Terence Tao recently remarked that with the latest AI models now apparently able to prove some of the most difficult mathematical theorems, mathematics has entered into an age of “proof abundance,” which makes knowing the answer to a problem much cheaper. In this new age, Tao emphasizes the importance of insight, encouraging mathematicians to understand problems as “lighthouses: not destinations to be reached in and of themselves, but as useful guides to explore the mathematical landscape” (Tao 2026). The problem itself is less important than how the process of grappling with that problem can illuminate mathematics.
An answer can play a role analogous to a problem. As an optimization problem with a strictly concave objective function, maximizing the growth rate in Equation 2 is, per se, straightforward: it requires no understanding of incompleteness, risk-neutral measures, numeraires, or any of the information-theoretic machinery that we developed. To find the optimal portfolio – to answer the problem – a few lines of Python code will do. Once we have found \(w^*\), we can then calculate our edge, \(W(w^*) - \ln r\), and other related quantities, such as the stranded growth, \(\sigma = W(w_{G'}^*) - W(w_{G}^*)\). What’s missing in all of this isn’t the answer; it is a deeper understanding of the structure of that answer, which, inter alia, helps us to ask better questions and to understand how disparate concepts relate to each other. For example, in this post I have shown how, as far as \(W(w^*)\) is concerned, \(p\) only matters in relation to its distance from \(\mathcal{Q}\), measured as a KL divergence. The important role of \(\mathcal{Q}\) would stay hidden from the practitioner who only cares about “the answer.”
As we saw in Equation 10, the dual problem of maximizing the growth rate over all portfolios \(w \in \mathcal{A}\) is the minimization of \(D(p \| q)\) over \(q \in \mathcal{Q}\), up to the additive constant \(\ln r\). This switches our focus from portfolios to probability distributions, and, because the discrepancy is a KL divergence, it has an exact reading in terms of data compression. This is because the redundancy (the expected excess number of bits) of an ideal code optimized for a model \(q\) when the data is generated by a source \(p\) is precisely \(D(p \| q) / \ln 2\) bits per symbol. The mean code length is then \(\frac{1}{\ln 2}(H(p) + D(p \| q))\) bits, where \(H(p) = -\sum_i p_i \ln p_i\) is the entropy of \(p\). Saying there is an edge, i.e. \(D(p \| q^*) > 0\), is therefore equivalent to saying no ideal code constructed from a risk-neutral measure can maximally compress the random data generated by \(p\): the mean code length is greater than the entropic minimum.
We have seen that information theory provides precise answers to both of the questions posed in the Introduction. Here is a recap of some of the more important points:

If your belief \(p\) is indeed the true distribution, then your edge is the redundancy of the code optimized for the closest risk-neutral measure to \(p\) in KL divergence (Equation 6) – and you have one if and only if at least one of your traded assets has a non-zero expected excess return under \(p\). \(D(p \| q)\) is what I’ve called the naive edge because it overstates your (actual) edge whenever \(q \neq q^*\). The excess, called the misfit, is a phantom edge (Equation 14): it is the redundancy caused by using a code optimized for \(m(q, w^*)\), which is the reverse information projection of \(p\) onto \(\mathcal{M}_{q,\,\cdot}\) (the set of tilted measures sharing the risk-neutral measure \(q\)).
If your belief \(p\) might not be the true distribution, then your edge is a competition between how well codes optimized for \(p\) and \(q^*_p\) respectively compress data drawn from the true distribution \(\tau\) (Equation 7).
Trading a new asset is helpful if and only if that asset is mispriced by \(q_G^*\) (Equation 20). Improving the Sharpe ratio (or equivalently, having non-zero alpha) is neither necessary nor sufficient (Table 1).
The usefulness of a new asset depends not on how much it reduces market incompleteness (how much it shrinks \(\mathcal{Q}\)) but on how far it moves the reverse information projection \(q^*\), which is seen most clearly in Equation 23. The additional growth that comes from trading a new asset – the stranded growth – is the misfit from using the risk-neutral measure in the enlarged market that is closest to \(p\) (in KL divergence) and the original market’s optimal portfolio (Equation 22). The stranded growth is a misfit from the perspective of the original market or a growth shortfall from the perspective of the expanded market.
Under certain conditions, the growth that is unlocked by trading an additional asset is well approximated by one half of the squared appraisal ratio of that asset (Equation 24).

As in my first post, I have made a number of simplifying assumptions, which help to clarify the core issues and ideas, but which do not reflect markets as they exist in reality. Among them: returns are i.i.d.; \(p\) is stationary and known (except in the discussion surrounding Equation 7); there are finitely many states; there are no demanding clients withdrawing their investments at inconvenient times; I have imposed no limits on leverage or shorting; I have not even mentioned transaction costs or trading frictions. In addition, my no-arbitrage assumption would need to be strengthened in continuous-time settings, as the equivalence between no arbitrage, the existence of an equivalent martingale measure, and the existence of a log-optimal portfolio no longer holds in general (see Delbaen and Schachermayer 1994 on no free lunch with vanishing risk; Karatzas and Kardaras 2007 on no unbounded profit with bounded risk).
I have also assumed that our goal is to maximize the growth rate by rebalancing \(w\) after each period. Not everyone will share this objective (Samuelson 1979).
My first post was about the importance of the concavity of the logarithm appearing in the growth rate and how, as an extreme example, that concavity can be harnessed to profitably trade assets that are provably going to zero, without ever shorting anything. In that post I assumed a complete market, which of course is rarely the case in reality. In this post, I rolled back that assumption, generalized the results of the first post, and hopefully provided some useful insight into how growth rates depend on market incompleteness. I intend to roll back other assumptions in future posts.

Provenance and further reading
Most of the ingredients used here are known, at least those found in What your disagreement with the market is worth, but are scattered across various literatures. The references I mention below (and the references therein) often discuss multiple overlapping topics, so if I recommend a source for one purpose below, keep in mind that it might have other material pertinent to this post. If you think I have missed any particularly important citations, please let me know.
For further reading on the relationship between information theory and investing, a good first source is Cover and Thomas (2006). Chapter 6 considers the case of complete markets (indeed \(G\) is diagonal there), where in Section 6.1 you can find a version of my Equation 7. Chapter 16 considers long-only log-optimal portfolios in further depth. Section 16.2 derives an analogue of Equation 3 and Equation 4 for long-only portfolios. By contrast, Breiman (1961) is a classic and early source for log-optimal investing that emphasizes probabilistic properties rather than connections to information theory.
The relationship between log-optimal investing and optimal portfolios as numeraires is investigated, among other places, in Long (1990). A deeper look into changes of numeraires and their applications in finance can be found in Geman et al. (1995). The special relationship between log-optimal investing and numeraires is also considered in Korn and Schäl (2009) and Karatzas and Kardaras (2007).
A proof of the Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing (FTAP) in a finite setting can be found in Harrison and Pliska (1981).
For a modern and comprehensive (though not especially technical) introduction to stochastic discount factors, numeraires, equivalent martingale measures, utility maximization, and related ideas, see Cochrane (2005).
Many of the results in What your disagreement with the market is worth, such as Equation 16 and Equation 14, can be found (or are implicit) in a very recent arXiv preprint (Vecer 2026). Among other things, the author there compares the forward \(\min_q D(q \| p)\) (the “I-projection” of Csiszár 1975) and reverse information projections \(\min_q D(p \| q)\) (the “reverse I-projection” of Csiszár and Matúš 2003) in our context, finding that only the latter commutes with a change of numeraire. N.B.: Vecer uses “forward” and “reverse” differently than I do.
Incompleteness complicates the analysis of markets; for more information in a discrete-time, finite setting see He and Pearson (1991). See also Harrison and Pliska (1981). For the reader interested in generalizations of these ideas to continuous-time settings, a good reference is Kramkov and Schachermayer (1999).
The upper bound on the growth rate (Equation 9) is really just weak duality in optimization, where the KL divergence comes from the dual problem of maximizing the growth rate. For more on bounds on the growth rate see Bansal and Lehmann (1997), who showed that the negative expectation of the log of an SDF is always an upper bound for the growth rate and that the bound is tight using the log-optimal portfolio as numeraire. In our setting any strictly positive SDF can be written as \(\frac{q_i}{rp_i}\), whence their inequality immediately implies Equation 9. The upper bound \(D(p \| q)\) appearing in Equation 9 is a particular instance of what Backus et al. (2014) call the entropy associated with an SDF that results whenever the SDF is proportional to \(\frac{q}{p}\). That \(D(p \| q)\) is an upper bound on what I’m calling the edge can also be found in Vecer (2026).
My derivation of the approximation for \(\sigma\) in What a missing asset is worth relies upon a result in Treynor and Black (1973).
For the reader interested in learning more about Géricault’s painting or the disaster it immortalized, a good place to start is Julian Barnes’ “Shipwreck” (Barnes 1989). In 1817 two of the survivors published a vivid, first-hand account of the disaster, which was translated into English the following year under the title Narrative of a Voyage to Senegal in 1816 (Savigny and Corréard 1818). For a thorough modern history, see Jonathan Miles’ The Wreck of the Medusa: The Most Famous Sea Disaster of the Nineteenth Century (Miles 2007). For the reader more interested in Géricault’s painting and the placement of a Black man at the apex of the human pyramid, see The Raft of the Medusa: Géricault, Art, and Race (Alhadeff 2002). The shipwreck and its aftermath generated an enormous amount of documentation, which the French government makes publicly available (Service historique de la Défense 2026).

title: 1: Shannon’s Demon, Made Exact
text:
If intuition is any guide, it shouldn’t be possible for a long-only portfolio to be profitable when each of its component assets is a lemon, unless, of course, one is clairvoyant and can predict those fleeting moments when random chance will favor each asset. Yet, as I’ll demonstrate in this post, not only is it possible to do this without any clairvoyance whatsoever, but also an investor can (almost surely) guarantee an exponential amount of money in the long run from an appropriately constructed portfolio of such lemons, at least under certain conditions that this post makes exact. It turns out that information theory provides a lovely explanation for why this is possible. The culmination of this post is a simple, closed-form formula for the excess expected growth rate of a portfolio over the risk-free rate, for a two-state, two-asset complete market. This formula is expressed as the difference between two Kullback-Leibler divergences.
